title: Scheduler max_num_seqs, token caps, KV hit-rate & on-prem guardrails
summary: Deep technical session to tune Redwood scheduler and batcher parameters for a regulated on-prem deployment. Focus on max_num_seqs, token limits, KV cache hit-rate, quantization tradeoffs, and security/air-gap constraints. Agreed next steps include a 10k-token long-tail throughput bench, sharing knobs guide, and pilot pricing.
next_steps: Avery to send scheduler knobs doc and example configs by 2025-11-07
Customer to provide token length distribution CSV and 2 week traffic traces
Run 10k-token long-tail benchmark on dedicated pilot pool and report latency/throughput tradeoffs
Schedule on-prem deployment checklist call (include security team) for week of 2025-11-17
action_items: Avery Chen: send scheduler knobs guide and quantization matrix by 2025-11-07
Maya Patel: upload token-length distribution + sample logs to S3 link by 2025-11-10
Rafael Ortiz: prepare a 1hr bench run script and baseline config for 10k token tests by 2025-11-12
Darren Li: confirm on-prem hardware (8x A100 80GB) and network egress constraints by 2025-11-13
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-04 14:30 UTC | Duration 72m | Attendees: Avery Chen, Rafael Ortiz, Samira Kahn - Redwood; Maya Patel, Darren Li, Priya Nair, Evan Ross - BlueForge

00:00 Avery Chen: okay everyone thanks for carving out the time. we wanted to focus today on throughput tuning for your on-prem pilot, specifically continuous batching and the scheduler knobs like max_num_seqs and token caps. Rafael's going to share some perf numbers and then we'll talk guardrails for long-tail requests.
00:22 Rafael Ortiz: hey hi, quick note, some of my numbers are from our internal runs so expect slight variance versus your environment, but they illustrate the knobs.
00:35 Maya Patel: sounds good, we saw big latency spikes when users paste long clinical notes (like 6-8k tokens) so that long-tail is our biggest issue.
00:45 Rafael Ortiz: yep, the classic tail. so two levers: one is max_num_seqs — how many concurrent sequences we pack in a batch — and the other is token_limit per request or soft caps with streaming. increasing max_num_seqs up to a point improves throughput but you'll see tail latency grow if a single seq has very long length.
01:12 Darren Li: can you define "point"? like numbers? our initial runs are on 8x A100 and we plan to keep most requests under 512 tokens but occasional 8k spikes.
01:25 Rafael Ortiz: sure. on an A100-80 with our current optimized kernels, typical sweet spot for chat-like workloads is max_num_seqs=32-64 depending on model size and kv cache behavior. if you set max_num_seqs=128 you may get better GPU utilization for uniform 256-token traffic but a single 8k request will force many batches to wait and tail latency explodes.
01:53 Samira Kahn: also note the continuous batching heuristic: we use dynamic batching windows which try to maximize utilization while honoring latency SLOs. you can tune windows, max_wait_ms, and max_batch_tokens. for on-prem with predictable network, bumping max_wait_ms slightly helps throughput.
02:16 Priya Nair: from a security perspective we need deterministic latency for some workloads — can we enforce upper bounds even if throughput suffers?
02:24 Rafael Ortiz: yes you can enforce hard token caps at the gateway (e.g., reject >4096 tokens) or we provide soft caps where long requests get routed to a prewarmed dedicated pool so they don't stall multi-tenant batches. tradeoff is cost.
02:43 Evan Ross: prewarmed pool meaning reserved GPUs with lower packing?
02:48 Rafael Ortiz: exactly — dedicated capacity with a conservative max_num_seqs, maybe 8-16, and a higher token_limit. That isolates long-tail from bursty 256-token traffic.
03:05 Maya Patel: ok that might work. but how do we keep KV cache hit-rate high? long sequences mess with KV eviction.
03:13 Rafael Ortiz: good question. KV cache hit-rate is influenced by prefix sharing and session affinity. if your app keeps session context per user, we see high hit-rates. For on-prem, we recommend sticky routing by session id and a KV cache size tuned to expected concurrent seqs and seq length. eviction policy should be LRU with per-session buckets to prevent thrash.
03:35 Darren Li: is there a rule of thumb for KV size?
03:39 Rafael Ortiz: estimate worst-case tokens in flight: concurrent_sessions * avg_seq_len * kv_entry_size. we published a spreadsheet but a quick rule: for 1k concurrent sessions at avg 512 tokens, allocate cache for ~512k tokens worth of KV entries. if memory hits, quantization for KV decreases size but also impacts perf slightly.
04:03 Maya Patel: we also have a compliance requirement to not retain raw prompts beyond 30 days. how is KV handled?
04:11 Samira Kahn: KV entries are ephemeral and tied to runtime; they are never written to disk. for our private deploy we can ensure KV RAM is scrubbed on session termination and add audited logs for when keys are evicted. we can also integrate with your key management policies for encryption at rest for config artifacts.
04:33 Priya Nair: on the encryption note, we need KMS integration and HSM support for on-prem — is that in scope?
04:38 Avery Chen: yes, Redwood Private includes KMS/HSM integrations and we can walk through keys, but for air-gapped installs we'll map to customer-managed HSM or attestation. we'll file that as an action item.
04:55 Rafael Ortiz: back to throughput: quantization helps reduce memory and increase throughput, but be careful with int8/int4 on certain layers; sometimes int4 gives weird output divergence for instruction-following prompts. we recommend model-aware quant profiles: int8 for dense, int4 for matmul heavy after eval. We can share recommended profiles per model.
05:23 Maya Patel: have you observed quantization causing more variance in latency?
05:27 Rafael Ortiz: minor variance. quantization can speed kernel execution, lowering per-token time, but kernel selection sometimes falls back to slower paths if mixed precision not supported on that GPU stack. test per model.
05:40 Darren Li: any scheduler knobs beyond max_num_seqs and max_wait_ms?
05:45 Rafael Ortiz: yes — max_batch_tokens, max_batch_size, per-tenant caps, preemption policies, and a token_guardrail layer that predicts cost of packing sequences vs latency and will split or route requests. we also have a scheduler setting called "seq_priority" to weight shorter sequences higher when chasing p95.
06:08 Evan Ross: interesting. does seq_priority harm throughput?
06:11 Rafael Ortiz: it can, if you bias too strongly for latency you reduce packing efficiency. the recommended approach: set target latency SLO and let the scheduler optimize; if you need hard SLOs then dedicate capacity.
06:25 Maya Patel: about token_guardrail — what heuristics do you use to split a long document? e.g., clinical note should not be naively chunked.
06:34 Rafael Ortiz: correct — semantic-aware chunking is ideal. we provide a plugin hook where you can supply a chunker that splits on section boundaries, preserves entities, and returns chunk metadata for reassembly. If you can't do semantic chunking, default is sliding window with overlap. but for clinical notes we'd recommend your preprocessing service to produce chunks and metadata before send.
07:00 Priya Nair: on audits, we need to see when a session was evicted and why. do you log KV evictions?
07:06 Samira Kahn: yes we can emit audit events: eviction_reason, session_id, timestamp. those logs can be forwarded to your SIEM. for Private we retain control plane logs in customer S3 or syslog per policy.
07:20 Maya Patel: can we simulate the 8k spikes in a bench? we can generate synthetic traces but want to mimic production-ish patterns.
07:27 Rafael Ortiz: please provide token length distribution and inter-arrival times; we have a bench harness that will replay with preserved timestamps and jitter. we saw that a small tail of 0.5% requests being >4k tokens increases p99 by 3-6x unless isolated.
07:44 Darren Li: what's the recommended config for mixed workloads? our baseline: 70% <256 tokens, 25% 256-1024, 5% >1024.
07:54 Rafael Ortiz: for that mix: recommended default pool: max_num_seqs=48, max_batch_tokens=65536, max_wait_ms=12, seq_priority=0.2 (favor shorter sequences slightly). then a dedicated long-tail pool with max_num_seqs=12, higher token_limit (8k), and prewarmed instances to avoid cold-starts.
08:18 Evan Ross: can we auto-scale dedicated pool on spikes? we worry about cost.
08:22 Rafael Ortiz: you can autoscale with a minimum reserve and burst capacity, but scaling GPUs takes time. we suggest buffer capacity and request-based routing: if dedicated pool full, route to hosted fallback with redaction or truncated view, depending on compliance.
08:36 Priya Nair: fallback to hosted is a no-go for PHI data.
08:39 Avery Chen: understood — for PHI you must use Private only; we can set hard rejects and provide human-in-the-loop alerts if a request exceeds limits.
08:50 Maya Patel: one more on KV: if we shard cache per-model vs global, what are the pros/cons?
08:56 Rafael Ortiz: sharding per-model gives predictable memory usage and reduces cross-model eviction. global cache uses memory more efficiently if models share prefixes but risks noisy neighbors. for regulated workloads, per-model sharding plus per-tenant quotas is simpler to audit.
09:13 Darren Li: and what about telemetry — how do we measure KV hit-rate in real-time?
09:18 Samira Kahn: we emit per-request metrics: kv_hits, kv_misses, kv_evictions, avg_kv_latency. dashboard shows hit-rate heatmaps by session and by model. we also provide sampling traces for KV keys to debug thrash.
09:33 Maya Patel: can we set proactive eviction policies if hit-rate drops below 60%? like rebuild cache or increase prewarm?
09:40 Rafael Ortiz: yes, you can set automated remediation: increase pool size, trigger cache warming, or spin up a temporary pool. we can wire that into your ops playbooks.
09:50 Evan Ross: any gotchas with network egress on-prem? we have intermittent peering to cloud for monitoring.
09:55 Samira Kahn: keep control plane connectivity minimal; data plane can be fully internal. for cloud control plane we support an air-gapped control plane proxy or you can run the control plane in your VPC.
10:08 Priya Nair: we will need an on-prem compliance checklist and attestation docs.
10:12 Avery Chen: we'll share our Private deployment checklist and the attestation template. action item noted.
10:20 Maya Patel: quick question on token_limit vs streaming: could we stream tokens to reduce per-request memory and keep latency tighter?
10:28 Rafael Ortiz: streaming is good: cut off large outputs into chunks and send partial responses; for long inputs, incremental encoding and partial KV usage helps. streaming complicates ordering and reassembly but our runtime supports it and it's a recommended approach for interactive large outputs.
10:44 Darren Li: what about prefetching KV for likely next tokens? is there any lookahead optimization?
10:50 Rafael Ortiz: we have a prediction-based prefetch where if session has a high chance to continue we keep KV warmed; it's heuristic-driven and can be enabled for sessions with high continuity. it costs memory but reduces tail.
11:05 Maya Patel: ok, say we accept some latency for the majority but must cap p99 to X ms — you recommended dedicated pool. can you propose an initial pilot config?
11:14 Rafael Ortiz: pilot config suggestion: default pool (handles 95%): max_num_seqs=48, max_batch_tokens=65536, max_wait_ms=12. long-tail pool (handles spikes): 2 nodes (8xA100 each) prewarmed, max_num_seqs=12, token_limit=8192, reserved memory for KV = 256GB. set auto-remediation: if long-tail queue > 8, scale to 3 nodes.
11:44 Evan Ross: price estimate rough?
11:46 Avery Chen: we'll send pilot pricing separate but ballpark for that dedicated on-prem reserve we'll include infra licensing and support.
11:54 Priya Nair: one last question: are there safe defaults for max_num_seqs for smaller GPUs like 40GB cards?
12:01 Rafael Ortiz: for 40GB an advisable range is 16-32 depending on model; reduce max_batch_tokens accordingly. also quantization helps fit larger batch sizes but again test per model.
12:12 Maya Patel: can you also include example JSON configs we can drop into our deploy?
12:17 Rafael Ortiz: yes — we'll attach example pools, scheduler knobs, and the token-guardrail rules.
12:24 Avery Chen: let's go to recap and next steps.
12:28 Rafael Ortiz: recap: 1) use mixed pool approach (default + dedicated long-tail) 2) start with recommended numbers (48/12) and tune after bench 3) prefer per-model KV sharding for auditability 4) use session stickiness to improve KV hit-rate 5) consider streaming + semantic chunking for very long inputs 6) quantization profiles per model — test in bench.
12:58 Maya Patel: that sounds right, appreciate it.
13:04 Priya Nair: thanks, please include attestation docs in follow-up.
13:07 Avery Chen: will do. any other questions?
13:10 Evan Ross: none here.
13:12 Avery Chen: great, we'll wrap.

Action recap (recorded): Avery to send knobs & pricing; Rafael to prepare bench script; Maya upload traces; Darren confirm HW.

End of transcript.
